Algebra I · Lesson 2.1

The Distributive Property

Solve this lesson →All lessons

Chapter 1 ended on a promise. 1.4 called two expressions equivalent when they agree at every value, and said the rules for rewriting one form into another would arrive in Chapter 2. This lesson delivers the first one, and it begins as a way to multiply ugly numbers in your head.

Problem
Compute 9⋅2049⋅204 in your head. The number 204204 splits into 200+4200+4, and each piece is easy to multiply by 99. Multiply both pieces, then add. What do you get?
Show a hint
  • Multiply the easy pieces, 9⋅2009⋅200 and 9⋅49⋅4, then add the two results.
Show the full solution
9⋅200=18009⋅200=1800 and 9⋅4=369⋅4=36, so the total is 1800+36=18361800+36=1836​. Splitting a number into easy pieces beats grinding through it digit by digit.
Key idea
The distributive property. For any numbers, a(b+c)=ab+aca(b+c)=ab+ac. The reason is that one count can be taken two ways. Take aa groups, each holding b+cb+c items. Counting whole groups gives a(b+c)a(b+c) items. Counting the bbs and the ccs separately gives ab+acab+ac. Both count the same items, so the totals match. That is what the last problem did with 9(200+4)9(200+4). The rules in 1.3 each concerned a single operation. This is the first one connecting addition and multiplication. As an instruction it says the outside factor multiplies each inside piece.
Problem
Compute 6⋅3986⋅398 the same way, but treat 398398 as 400−2400−2. Multiply each piece by 66, then correct for the extra. What is the product?
Show a hint
  • Round 398398 up to 400400, multiply, then pay back the 6⋅26⋅2 you borrowed.
Show the full solution
6⋅400=24006⋅400=2400 and 6⋅2=126⋅2=12, so the product is 2400−12=23882400−12=2388​. The correction comes off rather than on, since 398398 sits 22 below 400400.
Key idea
Distribution over subtraction. The form a(b−c)=ab−aca(b−c)=ab−ac is not a second law. By 1.3, subtracting cc is adding −c−c, so a(b−c)=a(b+(−c))=ab+a(−c)=ab−aca(b−c)=a(b+(−c))=ab+a(−c)=ab−ac, the same property applied to a sum. The outside factor multiplies each inside piece, and each piece keeps the sign it came with. In 6(400−2)6(400−2) the second piece is −2−2, which is why the 1212 was subtracted rather than added.
Problem
Nothing in the rule requires the inside pieces to be plain numbers. Expand 7(n+6)7(n+6). The result has two terms, one with nn and one without. Enter the constant term of the result, the term with no nn.
Show a hint
  • The 77 multiplies both pieces inside, the nn and the 66, not just the first.
Show the full solution
Distributing to both pieces gives 7⋅n+7⋅6=7n+427⋅n+7⋅6=7n+42, so the term with no nn is 4242​. Writing 7n+67n+6, with the 77 multiplying only the first piece, is the classic mistake.
Key idea
Expanding. Rewriting 7(n+6)7(n+6) as 7n+427n+42 is called expanding, and the outside factor multiplies every term inside. The two expressions are equivalent, meaning they are equal at every value of nn. In 1.4, 6(t+2)6(t+2) and 6t+126t+12 matched at one input, a good sign but not a proof. One application of the distributive property proves it, 6(t+2)=6t+126(t+2)=6t+12 at every tt. Checking values can only disprove a claim. Note that an expanded result has a coefficient and a constant term, so enter the part the question names.
Problem
Expand 5(3w−4)5(3w−4). The first inside piece already carries a coefficient, and the second carries a minus sign. Enter the coefficient of ww in the result.
Show a hint
  • The minus belongs to the 44. Multiply 55 by 3w3w, then 55 by −4−4, keeping that sign.
Show the full solution
5⋅3w=15w5⋅3w=15w and 5⋅(−4)=−205⋅(−4)=−20, so the result is 15w−2015w−20 and the coefficient of ww is 1515​. The minus stays attached to the 44, which is what keeps the constant at −20−20.
Problem
Expand g(g+11)g(g+11). The outside factor is now the variable itself, and 1.5 already settled what g⋅gg⋅g is. Enter the coefficient of the plain-gg term of the result, not the g2g2 term.
Show a hint
  • By 1.5, g⋅g=g2g⋅g=g2. The other product is g⋅11g⋅11.
Show the full solution
Distributing gives g⋅g+g⋅11=g2+11gg⋅g+g⋅11=g2+11g. The plain-gg term is 11g11g, so its coefficient is 1111​. The g2g2 term has a coefficient too, namely 11, but it belongs to the other term.
Key idea
The outside factor can be a variable. The rule holds for any numbers, and a variable stands for a number, so the factor outside the parentheses can be a letter, as in g(g+11)=g⋅g+g⋅11=g2+11gg(g+11)=g⋅g+g⋅11=g2+11g. Here g⋅g=g2g⋅g=g2 by 1.5's count of factors, and g⋅11g⋅11 is written 11g11g with the coefficient first. Every term inside still gets multiplied, whether the outside factor is a number, a letter, or a larger expression.
Problem
A student expands 8(y+3)8(y+3) and writes 8y+38y+3, multiplying only the first term inside. Evaluate both expressions at y=2y=2, each on its own. How far apart are their values?
Show a hint
  • Substitute y=2y=2 into 8(y+3)8(y+3) and into 8y+38y+3 separately, then compare the two numbers.
Show the full solution
At y=2y=2, the original is 8(2+3)=8⋅5=408(2+3)=8⋅5=40, while the student's version is 8⋅2+3=198⋅2+3=19, so the gap is 40−19=2140−19=21​. By 1.4, one input where two expressions disagree is enough to show they are not equivalent.
Key idea
Partial distribution. The most common expanding error is multiplying only the first term, claiming a(b+c)=ab+ca(b+c)=ab+c. That claim is false. Evaluating both sides at one convenient value gives two different outputs, which is the checking move from 1.6. A factor written next to parentheses multiplies every term inside, however many terms there are.
Problem
A bare minus sign directly in front of parentheses means multiplication by −1−1, so −(4d−7)−(4d−7) means (−1)(4d−7)(−1)(4d−7). Rewrite it by distributing that −1−1 over both inside terms. Enter the constant term of the result.
Show a hint
  • Both inside terms get multiplied by −1−1, so both signs flip, not just the first.
Show the full solution
Distributing hits both terms, (−1)(4d)=−4d(−1)(4d)=−4d and (−1)(−7)=+7(−1)(−7)=+7, so the result is −4d+7−4d+7 and the constant term is 77​. Flipping only the first sign, giving −4d−7−4d−7, is the standard error.
Key idea
Distributing −1−1. A bare minus in front of parentheses is multiplication by −1−1, so every sign inside changes. Positive terms become negative and negative terms become positive. This is the distributive property with a=−1a=−1, and since the product of two negatives is positive, the −7−7 inside came out as +7+7. Changing only the first sign is a common error. This comes up again in 2.4, which subtracts whole expressions.
Problem
The rule works for any number of inside terms. Compute 12(12+13+14)12(21​+31​+41​) by distributing the 1212 over all three terms. What value comes out?
Show a hint
  • Each product, 12⋅1212⋅21​, 12⋅1312⋅31​, and 12⋅1412⋅41​, is a whole number.
Show the full solution
12⋅12+12⋅13+12⋅14=6+4+3=1312⋅21​+12⋅31​+12⋅41​=6+4+3=13​. Adding the fractions first gives 13121213​ and lands in the same place, but distributing skips the common denominator entirely.
Problem
A number trick. Think of a number, add 55, triple the result, subtract 1515, then divide by 33. Start with 4747 and follow the four steps in order. What number comes out?
Show a hint
  • Follow the four steps one at a time, keeping each intermediate result.
  • When you finish, compare the number that came out with the number that went in.
Show the full solution
The steps take 4747 to 5252 to 156156 to 141141 and back to 4747​. Writing the start as nn, the first three steps build 3(n+5)−15=3n+15−15=3n3(n+5)−15=3n+15−15=3n, and dividing by 33 leaves nn, so whatever goes in comes back out.
Fun fact
When two parenthesized expressions multiply each other, as in (x+2)(x+3)(x+2)(x+3), the distributive property simply runs twice, once for each term of the first factor. That door opens with quadratics in Chapter 9.

The first rewriting tool is in hand. Ugly products split into easy pieces, and parentheses open without changing an expression's value at any input, which is exactly what 1.4 meant by equivalent. Next, 2.2 puts evaluation to work on heavier expressions, and in 2.3 this rule runs in reverse, reading ab+acab+ac as a(b+c)a(b+c), a move called factoring.

Practice these ideas

Practice
Mental math first. Compute 8⋅3068⋅306 in your head by splitting 306306 into 300+6300+6 and multiplying each piece by 88. Enter the product.
Show the solution
A common slip is to lose the middle zero and compute 8⋅36=2888⋅36=288, which is way too small for eight copies of a number near 300300. Keep the pieces as 300300 and 66. Then 8⋅300=24008⋅300=2400 and 8⋅6=488⋅6=48, so 8⋅306=2400+48=24488⋅306=2400+48=2448​.
Practice
Compute 4⋅9974⋅997 by treating 997997 as 1000−31000−3. Multiply each piece by 44, then correct for the overshoot. Enter the product.
Show the solution
Over subtraction the rule reads 4(1000−3)=4⋅1000−4⋅34(1000−3)=4⋅1000−4⋅3. Adding the correction instead of subtracting it gives 40124012, the wrong direction, since 997997 sits below 10001000. The product is 4000−12=39884000−12=3988​.
Practice
Expand 9(u+7)9(u+7) by multiplying each inside term by 99. Enter the constant term of the result, the term with no uu.
Show the solution
Multiplying only the first term gives 9u+79u+7, the partial-distribution error, and 9u+79u+7 is not equivalent to 9(u+7)9(u+7). The 99 multiplies the 77 as well, so the expansion is 9u+639u+63 and the constant term is 6363​.
Practice
Expand 6(5h−9)6(5h−9), keeping each inside term's sign as you distribute. Enter the coefficient of hh in the result, the number multiplying it.
Show the solution
Both products keep their signs, 6⋅5h=30h6⋅5h=30h and 6⋅(−9)=−546⋅(−9)=−54, so the expansion is 30h−5430h−54. Entering −54−54 answers the wrong part, and writing +54+54 loses the sign. The coefficient of hh is 3030​.
Practice
Expand t(t+17)t(t+17). The outside factor is a variable this time. Enter the coefficient of the plain-tt term of the result, not the t2t2 term.
Show the solution
The outside factor multiplies both terms, t⋅t=t2t⋅t=t2 and t⋅17=17tt⋅17=17t, so the expansion is t2+17tt2+17t. It is tempting to answer with the coefficient of t2t2, which is 11, or to type the whole term 17t17t, but the question asks only for the coefficient of the plain-tt term. That term is 17t17t, so the answer is 1717​.
Practice
Rewrite −(6p−19)−(6p−19) by distributing the minus. A bare minus in front of parentheses means multiplication by −1−1. Enter the constant term of the result.
Show the solution
Flipping only the first sign gives −6p−19−6p−19, the usual error. Multiplying each term by −1−1 gives −6p−6p and (−1)(−19)=+19(−1)(−19)=+19, so the result is −6p+19−6p+19 and the constant term is 1919​.
Practice
A student claims that 5(x+8)=5x+85(x+8)=5x+8. Settle it the 1.4 way, evaluate both expressions at x=3x=3. How far apart are their values?
Show the solution
At x=3x=3, 5(x+8)=5⋅11=555(x+8)=5⋅11=55 while 5x+8=15+8=235x+8=15+8=23. Entering 5555 or 2323 alone answers a different question, the ask is the gap between them. One disagreement proves the claim false, and the gap is 55−23=3255−23=32​.
Practice
Three terms and two letters this time. Expand 5(2a+9b−7)5(2a+9b−7), multiplying every term by 55. Enter the coefficient of aa.
Show the solution
The 55 multiplies all three terms, giving 10a+45b−3510a+45b−35. The ask names the coefficient of aa, so 4545 and −35−35 answer the wrong part. It is 5⋅2=105⋅2=10​.
Practice
Compute 15(23+25)15(32​+52​) by distributing the 1515 over both fractions. Done this way, no common denominator is needed.
Show the solution
Adding the fractions first gives 16151516​ and also works, but distributing skips the common denominator entirely. 15⋅23=1015⋅32​=10 and 15⋅25=615⋅52​=6, so the value is 10+6=1610+6=16​.
Practice
Compute 7⋅8.037⋅8.03 by splitting 8.038.03 into 8+0.038+0.03. Decimals distribute the same way whole numbers do. Enter the exact product.
Show the solution
The split gives 7⋅8=567⋅8=56 and 7⋅0.03=0.217⋅0.03=0.21. Misplacing the decimal point to get 2.12.1 ruins the sum, so keep 0.210.21 and the product is 56+0.21=56.2156+0.21=56.21​.
Practice
Expand 3(z2+6z+9)3(z2+6z+9). The inside has three terms, one of them squared, so the result has three terms too. Enter the constant term.
Show the solution
Every term gets the factor, so the expansion is 3z2+18z+273z2+18z+27. Stopping after two terms and leaving the 99 untouched is the partial-distribution error again. The constant term is 2727​.
Practice
Whatever number kk stands for, the expression 4(k+6)−4k4(k+6)−4k comes out to the same value every time. Enter that value.
Show the solution
The tempting slip is to distribute the 44 onto kk only and write 4k+6−4k4k+6−4k, which would leave 66. The 44 multiplies both terms inside the parentheses, so distributing gives 4k+24−4k4k+24−4k. The 4k4k and −4k−4k cancel completely, leaving 2424 no matter what kk is. That is the same cancellation that forced the number trick's output earlier in the lesson. The value is 2424​.
